rationale: B splits the work into nicely named helpers (parseDefinition, expand, exec), but its design is fragile. It stores definitions as expanded token lists and re-resolves those tokens against the dictionary at execution time. So if a definition uses a builtin such as `dup` and the user later redefines `dup`, the earlier definition silently picks up the new meaning, which contradicts its own comment about definition-time binding. Textual expansion can also blow up exponentially with nested definitions. A compiles each definition into a slice of closures resolved against the dictionary at definition time. That gives correct semantics for every redefinition case, with no expansion cost, and its dictionary of builtins as stack-transforming functions is a clean, idiomatic design. A's main loop with inline definition parsing is somewhat long, and the arithmetic closures repeat a little boilerplate. Even so, A is more robust and more soundly structured.
